subject: Tim Burton
hook: Why did Disney let Tim Burton go over a dog?
twist: The short Disney judged too dark for kids became a Disney-released stop-motion feature in 2012, still black and white, still PG.
mood: Black ink crosshatch storybook with lavender-grey washes and stop-motion clay texture (thumbprints, felt, miniature sets), cream paper margins. Music: sparse music-box and celesta over low cello drone, slow 70 bpm waltz, with a faint theremin wobble; warms slightly at the 2012 beat.
narration: Why did Disney let Tim Burton go over a dog? In nineteen eighty-four, Burton made a black-and-white short called Frankenweenie, about a boy who revives his dead dog. It got a PG rating. That reportedly ended Disney's plan to pair it with Pinocchio. Burton says the ratings board told him: "There's nothing you can cut. It's just the tone." Disney shelved the short, and Burton left, though he calls it a parting of ways. Paul Reubens had seen the short. Burton soon directed Pee-wee's Big Adventure. In twenty twelve, Disney released his feature-length stop-motion remake. Still black and white. Still PG. The film too dark for Disney became a Disney film. Too dark for kids, or just right?

captions.instagram_caption:
Why did Disney let Tim Burton go over a dog? 🐶

In 1984 Burton, a young Disney animator, made Frankenweenie: a black-and-white short about a boy who revives his dead pet.

It was rated PG, which reportedly scrapped the plan to show it with Pinocchio. Burton says the ratings board told him, "There's nothing you can cut. It's just the tone."

Disney shelved it and Burton moved on, though he describes it as a parting of ways. Paul Reubens had seen the short, and Burton went on to direct Pee-wee's Big Adventure.

In 2012 Disney released his feature-length stop-motion remake, still black and white, still PG.
